newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn, unions at odds over new German jobs summit.
newsitem.headline: Bonn, unions at odds over new German jobs summit.

text.p: German unions must drop their preconditions for a new "jobs summit" to combat naggingly high German unemployment before any new talks are planned, German Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt said on Sunday.
Rexrodt has hinted the goverment would be willing to discuss a second attempt of the so-called "Alliance for Jobs" initiative between unions, politicians and employers that failed in 1996.
But he said demands by German unions that terms of the first deal be fulfilled before any new talks would not be met.
"There will be no talks if there are preconditions," Rexrodt told Germany's Focus magazine.
Unions have demanded employers cut overtime payments to create new jobs, hire more part-time workers and end attacks on unions that negotiate nationwide industry wage deals.

A record two billion hours of overtime was posted in 1996 as German unemployment hovered around the post-unification record of four million throughout 1996, according to the German Federal Labour Office.

Dieter Schulte, head of the German Federation of Trade Unions (DGB), said at the weekend terms of the first "Alliance for Jobs" deal must be met before new talks aimed at reducing German jobless levels can be held.
DAG white-collar workers' union leader Roland Issen also told Focus magazine at the weekend that "a few signals" were needed to start a new round of talks.
The previous alliance, which in 1996 gained the support of unions, employers and the backing of government, sought to link wage moderation to job creation measures.

But it failed when the unions accused German Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government of betrayal by pushing through a package of austerity measures which, among other things, was designed to cut a number of labour-related social costs.
Kohl sparked more anger in October when he suggested that a halving of German unemployment was perhaps too optimistic.
In addition, Federal Labour Office President Bernhard Jagoda said a new round of talks should be held but also that 1997 wage deals must be lower to create new jobs.
But Schulte said it was time for companies to begin creating new jobs after unions gave in to lower wage concessions in return for additional jobs.
